newsitem.title: FINLAND: FEATURE - New captains of industry sharpen Finnish focus.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New captains of industry sharpen Finnish focus.

text.p: A recent reshuffle in forest industry flagship UPM-Kymmene may have started a major shift of Finnish business influence to a younger breed of industrialists away from older patrons.

Commentators see owners taking more control of leading industry, as a first step in longer-term cultural change to unravel a complex network of cross-holdings dating from an era when competition was milder than today.

The process is only just starting, but the new generals are all about 10 years younger than those they look scheduled to replace, born before World War Two and now around normal retirement age, in their sixties.

Among those apparently on the way out is tycoon Casimir Ehrnrooth -- leader of Finland's strongest capitalist family, which is often compared the Wallenberg dynasty in Sweden that controls a leading bank and huge stakes in major industries.

Ehrnrooth and his allies Tauno Matomaki and ex-Pohjola chairman Yrjo Niskanen were ousted from the helm of UPM in a corridor consensus move at the time of its last annual meeting: the decision never came to a vote.

They may yet stage a comeback, but if not, those now on their way in to Finland's most exclusive cabinets include Lauri Juhani Joukhi, head of the privately-owned trading group Thomesto Trading, who becomes UPM head.
Iiro Viinanen, a former finance minister and now head of insurer Vakuutusosakeyhtio Pohjola, and Merita Bank CEO Vesa Vainio, were both named deputy chairmen at UPM.
Insurer Sampo's CEO Jouko Leskinen and Jorma Ollila, head of telecoms giant Nokia, are also part of a new power cluster evolving in UPM's board, analysts say.
Viinanen built a reputation in the international investment community with a tight grip of state coffers, and moved to Pohjola, Finland's second biggest insurer, in 1996.

The Jouhki family are among Finland's leading private investors and have a reputation for a committed approach to ownership; and Merita's holdings in industry and insurance clearly entitle Vainio to various boardroom involvements.
"The tumult in UPM-Kymmene is the beginning of a significant generation changeover in the innermost cabinets of Finnish business," columnist Atte Jaaskelainen wrote in daily Helsingin Sanomat.
SIGNIFICANCE OF UPM
UPM has a central position in the complicated maze of cross-holdings in Finland's top industry (see table below), directly and through its significant holdings in Merita, Pohjola and Sampo.
Formed in 1995 through the merger of Repola (then led by Matomaki) and Kymmene (which Ehrnrooth then chaired), UPM is also Nokia's second-largest registered owner.
Merita and the insurers also have wide industry holdings, not least their stakes in UPM which now gave them control over the group's board.

Although analysts agree the recent shift may prove important, they say Finnish corporate culture still is a long way short of true corporate governance and thinking in terms of shareholder value, rather than old style "old boy" capitalism.

Aros Securities president Lauri Rosendahl said a good example of this back-scratching culture were various recent management options schemes, set at "too generous terms from the point of view of the shareholders".
He also said the old culture was still seen in the appointment of Nokia's Ollila to UPM's board, which could create clear conflicts of interest since UPM is a top owner.
"What is the value-added for UPM's shareholders in owning Nokia shares?" Rosendahl said. "If they want Nokia shares, they can buy them."
Jouhki told the daily Helsingin Sanomat he would be "chief coach" above the players in UPM and that this corresponded to his idea of a modern corporate governance thinking.
That was welcomed by Evli chief analyst Christian Kock.
"The important thing is that corporate governance comes to the foreground, with focus on direct ownership and competence," he said.
